entry.title: From Route 53 to Hostinger: Moving an AWS App to a New Domain Without Moving DNS

link.title: From Route 53 to Hostinger: Moving an AWS App to a New Domain Without Moving DNS

entry.content:
It started with what sounded like a small task:

“We’re moving the app to the new domain.”

The app runs on ECS behind an Application Load Balancer, and from day one the ALB was pointed straight at a domain in Route 53. An alias record to the ALB, ACM certificate validation, all of it neatly in Terraform. The new domain, though, was bought on Hostinger.

Same app, same load balancer, new name. How hard could it be?

Harder than “just point the domain somewhere,” it turns out. Everything Route 53 used to handle quietly for us, the certificate validation and the records pointing at the ALB, now had to be set up again by hand on the Hostinger side. A new certificate, a handful of CNAMEs, and a few surprises along the way.

I could have moved the nameservers to Route 53 and kept working the way I was used to. But that would have been a whole project of its own. The domain was already set up and managed on Hostinger, so it stayed there.

Which meant the real job was this: rebuild, on Hostinger, everything Route 53 used to do for us. Without breaking the old domain while the new one came to life.

Every domain in this post uses the .example TLD, so swap in your own.

What you give up when you leave Route 53

Route 53 does a lot of quiet work that you only notice once it’s gone.

Alias records become plain CNAMEs. In Hostinger, you point a CNAME at the ALB’s DNS name. Never an A record to the ALB’s IPs, because those change without notice.

The alias health check disappears. evaluate_target_health mostly matters for failover. With one ALB and no failover, users get a 503 either way when every target is down. I let this one go.

ACM validation turns manual. Terraform can’t create the validation record anymore, so someone has to copy it into Hostinger’s DNS zone editor. And it has to stay there, because ACM reuses it for auto-renewal.

The records leave your IaC. terraform plan won’t notice if someone edits them. I compensated with a Terraform output that prints exactly what to create, plus a short list in the infra repo’s README. Not as good as state, but better than memory.

The apex can’t be a CNAME. DNS doesn’t allow it, since the apex already holds SOA, NS, MX, and TXT records. So the app lives on app.new.example, and the bare domain gets a redirect from Hostinger instead.

None of these are dealbreakers. But they’re worth knowing before you commit, not after.

The setup, briefly

The AWS side is well documented, so I’ll keep this short. Same ALB, same target group, same ECS service. Four changes:

  1. A second ACM certificate, validated by hand. Without Route 53, ACM can’t add its validation CNAME for you, so it goes into Hostinger manually (AWS docs). Our Terraform module always created that record in Route 53, so I added a manage_validation_record flag that skips it and prints the record as an output instead.
  2. The new cert on the existing HTTPS listener. The ALB picks the right certificate per hostname via SNI, so the old cert stays the default and the new one sits beside it.
  3. A host rule right next to the old one. Priority 101, directly after the old host’s 100, so the new domain behaves exactly like the old one. A separate rule also makes cleanup a one-resource change later.
  4. A CNAME in Hostinger pointing app at the ALB’s DNS name. Before creating it, I tested everything with curl --resolve, forcing the new hostname onto one of the ALB’s IPs.

For a while both domains had to work, which meant two things I almost missed. CORS on the API and the upload bucket had to allow both origins. And the frontend’s API URL is baked in at build time, so switching it meant a rebuild, not a config change.

That set the order: cert, listener, CORS, DNS, frontend. Every step only adds. The one rule I wouldn’t bend is CORS before DNS, because the moment the new domain resolves, its frontend starts calling the API from a new origin.

The things no guide warned me about

This is the part I actually wanted to write down, because I couldn’t find it anywhere else.

The DNS panel “helpfully” appended the domain. ACM gives you the full record name, something like _a1b2c3.app.new.example. Paste that into the Name field and Hostinger’s DNS panel, like many others, adds the domain again, so you end up with _a1b2c3.app.new.example.new.example. Validation just… never completes. Enter only _a1b2c3.app, then check it with dig before you start waiting.

Terraform gave up long before ACM did. aws_acm_certificate_validation waits 75 minutes by default. ACM waits up to 72 hours. So slow DNS propagation or a late copy-paste makes Terraform time out while the certificate is perfectly fine. Rerunning apply picks it back up. Better yet, split it into two applies: one to create the cert and print the records, one to validate and attach. The real risk is the opposite case. Leave a wrong record for 72 hours, and the cert has to be requested again.

A local apply rolled out a placeholder image. In CI, the image tag comes in as a variable. Locally, it defaulted to placeholder so plan wouldn’t complain. My apply for a certificate and a listener rule also quietly created a new task definition pointing at an image that didn’t exist. Lesson learned: no defaults on variables like that, and read the plan to the end. A task definition change in the middle of DNS work is a red flag.

An evening deploy woke the app while the database slept. This environment shuts down after hours. A scheduler stops RDS and scales ECS to zero. Terraform saw that desired_count didn’t match the code and “fixed” it. The app came up, the database didn’t, and the tasks restarted in a loop. Now desired_count sits in ignore_changes, and infra changes happen during working hours.

Don’t rush the cleanup

Once the new domain was stable, the tidy instinct was to delete everything old. I didn’t. The old domain still lives in bookmarks, sent emails, and third-party integrations, and its certificate costs nothing while it keeps auto-renewing through Route 53. When it’s time, switching the old rule to a 301 redirect is the gentler path.

The less technical part mattered just as much. Our ALB had no access logs, so I had no way to see who was still hitting the old domain. The only real safety net was telling people: the new domain, how long the old one stays up, and what to update. Bookmarks, env vars, webhooks, OAuth redirect URIs.

Why this was more than a DNS change

Here’s what I keep coming back to: the Terraform was the easy part. The hard part was everything Route 53 had been doing for us without anyone noticing. Alias records, certificate validation, renewals, all of it tracked in code. None of that moved with the domain. It all had to be rebuilt by hand, one CNAME at a time.

A domain move looks like a rename on paper. In practice, it’s a migration.

So if there’s one habit worth carrying into the next one, it’s this: before moving a domain, list what your current DNS setup quietly does for you. That list is your real migration plan.

entry.title: My First openSUSE.Asia Summit: Container Observability on openSUSE Tumbleweed

link.title: My First openSUSE.Asia Summit: Container Observability on openSUSE Tumbleweed

entry.content:
I spent October 3–4 in Yogyakarta at openSUSE.Asia Summit 2026, and I gave my first talk at an openSUSE event: Container Observability on openSUSE: A Practical Guide with Prometheus, cAdvisor, and Grafana.

This post is both my event report and a written version of the talk, so you can follow along even if you weren’t in the room.

Getting there

I travelled from Tabanan, Bali, by sleeper bus to Yogyakarta, and came home by train to Ketapang, then ferry and bus across to Bali. The trip was supported by the openSUSE Travel Support Program, paid through the Geeko Foundation. Thank you to the TSP team and the organizing committee. For a first-timer in this community, that support made the difference between “maybe next year” and actually showing up.

Why this talk

I work with Ubuntu-based infrastructure every day, and almost every “how to monitor Docker containers” tutorial assumes Ubuntu: apt, ufw, AppArmor. So I asked myself: what happens if I rebuild the same stack on openSUSE Tumbleweed? What breaks, what’s different, what’s easier?

Halfway through the session I noticed how many people had come, far more than I expected. I was nervous, but the questions afterwards made it worth it.

The stack in one picture

Three open-source tools, one pipeline:

  • cAdvisor reads each container’s cgroup statistics and serves them at /metrics on port 8080.
  • Prometheus scrapes that endpoint every 15 seconds and stores time series.
  • Grafana runs PromQL queries against Prometheus and draws the dashboards.

It’s a pull model over plain HTTP, so you can curl every step when debugging. I wanted per-container CPU, memory, network, and disk stored over time, because docker stats only shows the present, and a restarted container takes its numbers with it.

Building it on Tumbleweed

Docker comes straight from the openSUSE repositories, with no extra repo or GPG key:

sudo zypper refresh
sudo zypper install docker docker-compose
sudo systemctl enable --now docker
sudo usermod -aG docker $USER   # log out and in again

cAdvisor runs with read-only host mounts. I pin a version instead of using latest, and the image now lives on ghcr.io (older tutorials still point to gcr.io). I also don’t publish its port at all, because Prometheus reaches it by service name over the Compose network.

Prometheus needs only a short config:

global:
  scrape_interval: 15s
scrape_configs:
  - job_name: cadvisor
    static_configs:
      - targets: ["cadvisor:8080"]

Before building any dashboard, open the Prometheus Targets page and confirm the cadvisor job is UP.

For Grafana, add a Prometheus data source at http://prometheus:9090. Use the service name, not localhost, because Grafana runs inside a container. For a quick start, import community dashboard 14282.

Four queries that cover the basics

CPU, in cores:

sum by (name) (rate(container_cpu_usage_seconds_total{name!=""}[5m]))

Memory, in bytes:

sum by (name) (container_memory_working_set_bytes{name!=""})

Network receive, in bytes per second:

sum by (name) (rate(container_network_receive_bytes_total{name!=""}[5m]))

Disk writes, in bytes per second:

sum by (name) (rate(container_fs_writes_bytes_total{name!=""}[5m]))

Two habits worth keeping. Use rate() over 5 minutes, because these are counters. And filter name!=”” so host-level cgroups don’t clutter your view.

For memory alerts, use working set, not raw usage. container_memory_usage_bytes includes page cache the kernel can reclaim, so it often looks scarier than reality. Working set is much closer to what leads to an OOM kill.

In my demo, a container called cpu-hog runs an endless loop but is started with — cpus 0.5. The dashboard shows its CPU line sitting flat at exactly 0.5 cores: the cgroup limit at work, read by cAdvisor straight from the kernel.

What changed compared to Ubuntu

  • Packages: apt on Ubuntu, zypper on openSUSE.
  • Docker source: Docker’s own apt repo on Ubuntu, the openSUSE OSS repo on Tumbleweed.
  • Firewall: ufw on Ubuntu, firewalld on openSUSE.
  • Security module: AppArmor on Ubuntu, SELinux (enforcing on new installs) on Tumbleweed.
  • Root filesystem: ext4 on Ubuntu, Btrfs with Snapper snapshots on Tumbleweed.

The monitoring tools don’t care about the distro. What changes is the plumbing around them. Three things to check before you trust your dashboard:

1. SELinux labels. A bind-mounted config can fail with “permission denied”. Add :Z to the volume, confirm with ausearch -m avc, and keep SELinux enforcing.

2. Docker’s storage backend. On my Tumbleweed, Docker uses the containerd image store, so cAdvisor needs the containerd socket, which lives in /run/docker/containerd. My first run collected metrics but no container names, until I mounted that socket.

3. Published ports. Docker writes its own firewall rules, so a published port can be reachable even when firewalld doesn’t list it. I saw this myself: Grafana on port 3000 was open to the internet while firewalld only allowed ssh. Bind Prometheus to 127.0.0.1, don’t publish cAdvisor, and change Grafana’s default admin password first.

One caveat: I tested all this on a minimal Tumbleweed install on a cloud server with a public IP, not on a laptop. A minimal install has no sudo or SELinux tools by default, and on a public server, port exposure matters much more than on a VM behind NAT.

Takeaways

  • The stack stays the same; openSUSE changes the plumbing.
  • Check SELinux labels, the storage backend, and published ports before trusting your numbers.
  • Start from dashboard 14282, then add your own PromQL panels.
  • If you’ve only used Ubuntu like me, try Tumbleweed. It was a lot less scary than I expected.

If you want to scale this beyond one host, Geraldhi Aditya Putra Mahayadnya’s summit talk on distributed monitoring with Prometheus and Thanos is the natural next step. Podman is my next experiment on Tumbleweed.

Everything from the talk, including the Compose file, Prometheus config, and dashboard, is here: https://github.com/sintiasnn/container-observability-opensuse

Slides: https://opensuse.github.io/slides/presentations/opensuse-asia-summit-2026-container-observability-on-opensuse-a-practic-ni-putu-sintia-wati.pdf

Thank you

Thank you to the openSUSE.Asia Summit 2026 organizing committee and volunteers for putting together such a welcoming event, and for accepting a first-time openSUSE speaker. Thank you also to the Travel Support Program and the Geeko Foundation for helping me get to Yogyakarta, and to everyone who came to my session and stayed for the questions.

Walking in, I was nervous. Walking out, I had a long list of things to try, starting with Podman on Tumbleweed. If you’re curious about openSUSE but have only used other distros, come say hi in the community. It’s a lot friendlier than I expected.

See you at the next summit!

entry.title: When “The Same Version” Isn’t: Setting Up My First Mobile CI/CD Pipeline

link.title: When “The Same Version” Isn’t: Setting Up My First Mobile CI/CD Pipeline

entry.content:
A cross-platform version-pinning bug that only shows up once your Android and iOS release jobs are both live — and the fix that made them agree on the same Flutter revision.

The Hook

One day, my pipeline threw this:

A release with version 1.0.0+107 already exists but was built using a different Flutter revision.
Existing release built with: 3.41.6 (abc1234)
Current release built with: 3.47.0 (def5678)

This showed up while I was setting up a mobile CI/CD pipeline for the very first time — and touching an iOS pipeline for the first time too. Two jobs, two platforms, both nominally building the “same” version. Turns out they weren’t.

This post is a record of the debugging process — not a plan I had going in, but something I genuinely found one failure at a time.

Why This Happens

The core insight I only got after a fair amount of debugging: a code-push tool (Shorebird, in this case) isn’t just something you invoke inside your existing CI toolchain. It vendors its own Flutter checkout, completely separate from whatever Flutter is baked into your image or runner.

So if your job runs inside an image with Flutter 3.41.6, that has zero effect on what Shorebird actually builds with — unless you explicitly tell it which version to use. Left unpinned, it silently defaults to whatever the latest stable Flutter it has mirrored is.

There’s a subtler constraint on top of that: the tool enforces that every platform under one release version must be built from the exact same Flutter revision. This constraint only becomes visible once two platforms (Android and iOS) both attempt a release for the same version — testing a single platform in isolation gives you false confidence that everything’s fine.

Timeline (As Discovered, Not As Planned)

This is my favorite part to tell, because none of it was anticipated up front — it was all found the hard way.

1. An invisible prerequisite. The very first job failed before any of this, because the CI image had no Node at all — so it wasn’t just the code-push tool that couldn’t run, supporting scripts (like the build-number generator) couldn’t either. Not the real fix, but nothing else moves without it.

2. Iteration 1 — looked right, was only half right. The Android job failed at the Gradle-plugin-apply step. Turned out the newer Flutter version (which the tool picked up unpinned) required a higher minimum Gradle version than what the project had pinned. First fix: read the Flutter version off the job’s own image and pass it explicitly to the code-push tool. Android-only.

3. Iteration 2 — ~19 hours later, and only then did it become clear why iteration 1 wasn’t enough. The iOS job failed too, but not on Gradle — on the cross-platform revision-lock check above. Why didn’t “read the version from the image” carry over to iOS? Because the iOS runner is bare-metal macOS, not a container — there’s no image tag to read a version from. Only at this point did it become clear the fix had to be platform-agnostic: one pinned file both jobs read, not “derive it from whatever environment this job happens to be in.”

Root Cause, In Short

Two independent facts colliding:

(a) The code-push tool’s Flutter is out-of-band from your CI image’s Flutter, and defaults to “latest stable” when unpinned.

(b) The tool enforces Flutter-revision consistency across platforms for a given release version — something a single-platform pipeline will never catch.

The Fix

A single version-pin file at the repo root, read by both platform jobs through a shared CI template, validated against a strict format check that hard-fails the job rather than silently proceeding with an empty string.

# flutter-version.json at repo root: { "flutter": "3.41.6" }
jobs:
  release-android:
    steps:
      - id: pin
        run: |
          FLUTTER_VERSION=$(jq -r .flutter flutter-version.json)
          [[ "$FLUTTER_VERSION" =~ ^[0-9]+\.[0-9]+\.[0-9]+$ ]] || { echo "bad version"; exit 1; }
          echo "flutter_version=$FLUTTER_VERSION" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
      - run: shorebird release android --flutter-version=$
  release-ios:
    steps:
      - id: pin
        run: |
          FLUTTER_VERSION=$(jq -r .flutter flutter-version.json)
          [[ "$FLUTTER_VERSION" =~ ^[0-9]+\.[0-9]+\.[0-9]+$ ]] || { echo "bad version"; exit 1; }
          echo "flutter_version=$FLUTTER_VERSION" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
      - run: shorebird release ios --flutter-version=$

One thing that’s easy to get wrong: the patch job (as opposed to release) deliberately does not use this pin.

# release jobs: pin --flutter-version explicitly (source of truth = repo file)
# patch jobs: this flag is DELIBERATELY omitted — the tool automatically
# inherits the revision the release being patched was built with.
# If a patch job followed the repo's current pin instead, a patch could
# silently target a different Flutter revision than the release it's
# patching was actually built with.

Bonus Root Cause: The Moving Gradle Floor

Flutter’s minimum required Gradle version shifts between minor releases. So a code-push-tool-side Flutter bump that looks completely harmless can break a project still pinned to an older Gradle wrapper — with zero lines of app code changed. This class of bug is confusing because the error looks like a Gradle problem, when the actual root cause is an unpinned Flutter version.

Side Story: A Build Number That Couldn’t Be Trusted From Any Single Source

The obvious first idea was to just read it from pubspec.yaml or the platform's official distribution CLI. Neither held up:

  • The official CLI used for Android distribution has no command to list releases that have already shipped — it can only push, not query.
  • pubspec.yaml itself, once checked, had drifted from what was actually live in the stores — not a hypothesis, a confirmed fact.

The fix: query the distribution platform’s REST API directly, page through every release that’s ever existed, filter out anything expired, take the highest surviving build number, and increment it.

function nextBuildNumber(distributionApi, fallbackFromManifest):
    releases = paginateAll(distributionApi.listReleases())
    nonExpired = releases.filter(r => !r.expired)
    if nonExpired.isEmpty():
        return fallbackFromManifest + 1   # brand-new app only
    highest = max(nonExpired, by: r => r.buildNumber)
    return highest.buildNumber + 1

This logic itself only became correct on the fourth attempt — an early version mistakenly used the CI pipeline’s own run number as the build number (jumping by thousands), and a later version forgot to exclude expired builds from the “highest” calculation.

Release vs. Patch: Who Decides?

Turns out it’s not automatic — and that’s a deliberate choice, not a tooling limitation. The code-push tool has a technical guard (it refuses to patch if the diff touches assets, native code, or dependencies), but the final call on “should this ship as a patch or a full release” stays a human judgment, because “is this diff Dart-only” isn’t something you want a heuristic guessing at — guessing wrong means shipping mismatched assets to production.

patch result:
  if diff touches: assets/, native code, dependencies
    => REFUSE ("ship a full release instead")
  else
    => proceed (Dart-only patch)
  # a flag exists to force past this guard — treat it as a documented
  # footgun, not a normal escape hatch

Lessons

  • A deploy tool that vendors its own toolchain has a second version-resolution system you must pin explicitly — don’t assume “my CI image already pins the version” covers it.
  • A constraint that only surfaces when two independent pipelines converge (here: two platforms, two runner types) won’t show up until you actually run both — testing a single job gives false confidence.
  • “Derive the fix from the local environment” (an image tag) is a trap when your job types don’t share an environment (container vs. bare-metal runner) — prefer a single file both read instead.
  • When a vendor CLI has no introspection/list command, you’ll end up reverse-engineering its REST API — budget time for it, and expect it to take a few correctness passes (pagination, excluding expired entries, etc.), not to work on the first try.

entry.title: Downsizing Infra When the IDR Drops: Why “Just Turn Off Idle Resources” Isn’t the Whole Story

link.title: Downsizing Infra When the IDR Drops: Why “Just Turn Off Idle Resources” Isn’t the Whole Story

entry.content:
It started with a simple question from my manager:

“Why did our AWS cost get this bad last month?”

Not a demand to cut costs. Just an ask to analyze — figure out what actually happened. That question sent me down a rabbit hole, because the honest answer wasn’t one clean root cause. It was a mix of things, and the IDR was sitting right in the middle of it.

Here’s the thing: our cloud bills are in USD, but our budget is in IDR. When the exchange rate moves against us, the same infra that was “fine” last quarter suddenly eats a noticeably bigger chunk of the plan, even if nothing on our end actually changed.

That’s when the instruction that usually follows kicks in: downsize dev infra, cut costs.

Simple enough on paper. In practice? Not even close.

The advice everyone gives (and why it only half-works)

If you Google “cloud cost optimization,” you’ll get the same three tips every time: turn off idle resources, use spot instances, rightsize your instances. Solid advice — for the right workload, at the right time.

But here’s what nobody tells you: “idle” is doing a lot of heavy lifting in that sentence.

In a dev environment where a feature ships almost every day, nothing is ever really idle. It’s active in the morning for testing, active in the afternoon for debugging, active in the evening for a demo to the PM. There’s no clean, safe window to just shut things down without stepping on someone’s work. And for a heavier service, one that takes real time to warm back up or reconnect to third-party integrations, spinning it back on costs more than money. It costs everyone’s time and momentum.

Spot instances have the same problem from a different angle. They’re cheap because the provider can yank the capacity back whenever they want, not when you want. Fine for a batch job that checkpoints itself. Not fine for a dev environment people are actively working in — an interruption there doesn’t save money, it just relocates the cost into lost focus and context-switching.

So the “textbook” moves don’t fail because they’re wrong. They fail because they assume a kind of stillness that a fast-moving project simply doesn’t have.

It’s not one infra, it’s many — and they don’t all deserve the same treatment

The other thing that gets lost in generic advice: a project isn’t one blob of infra. It’s a mix. A compute-heavy service that depends on third-party integrations, a lightweight internal API, a database holding actual state, a worker queue processing jobs. Each one has a completely different relationship with “downsizing.”

Squeeze the heavy service too hard and it just… can’t keep up with the third-party calls it depends on, or starts timing out. That’s not a cost saving, that’s an outage. Squeeze the lightweight API and probably nobody notices. Touch the database wrong and now you’re not optimizing cost, you’re risking data integrity.

Treating all of that with one blanket policy is how you end up cutting in the wrong place. The decision has to happen per component, not per project.

What actually changed how I approach this

My senior pushed me on something that reshaped how I think about all of this: decide from data, not from guessing.

It sounds obvious, but it’s easy to skip when you’re under pressure to cut costs now. The instinct is to eyeball it — “this instance feels oversized” — and just resize it. But without actually looking at CPU utilization, memory patterns, latency, and traffic over time, you’re gambling. And if it goes wrong, you don’t even have a clear reason why, which makes the next decision just as blind as the last one.

Data-driven downsizing means every cut is defensible. If someone asks “why did we drop this to X,” there’s a number behind the answer, not a shrug.

Infra needs a seat at the table before the project even starts

This is the part I’ve come to feel strongly about: cost problems that show up mid-project are often architecture problems that started at project kickoff.

If infra only gets brought in after the architecture is decided, we’re just there to provision what’s already been designed. By the time cost pressure hits, we’re stuck retrofitting savings onto a shape that was never built with cost or scalability in mind. Getting involved from the initial project declaration, helping shape the architecture around what this specific case actually needs, means fewer nasty surprises later. You’re not choosing between “keep the promised experience” and “cut the budget” as a last-minute panic. You designed for both from day one.

And it doesn’t stop at launch. Conditions keep shifting — new features, traffic spikes, changing load patterns — so monitoring has to be a loop, not a one-time check. Part of that loop is always having a plan B ready: if load spikes, what scales first; if we need to cut costs again, which component is safe to touch first, and which one absolutely isn’t.

Why this matters beyond the infra team

Here’s the thing that ties it all together for me: none of this lives in a vacuum. A PM isn’t just promising a client a finished feature — they’re promising an experience. How fast assets load, how responsive the app feels, how stable it is under load. All of that experience is sitting directly on top of the infra decisions we make.

So when cost pressure hits, downsizing isn’t just an internal “let’s save some money” call. It’s a call that can quietly break a promise someone already made to a client. That’s why the framework matters more than any single trick. Know which components tolerate being downsized. Know when, if ever, there’s a safe window to do it. And never lose sight of the experience riding on top of it all.

The IDR is going to keep doing what it does. What’s in our control is whether our decisions are based on data and a real understanding of the architecture — or just reacting to a number on a billing dashboard.

entry.title: Knowledge and Experience Don’t Always Live Where You Do

link.title: Knowledge and Experience Don’t Always Live Where You Do

entry.content:
hi! switching gears from technical writing for a bit :D this one’s more on the soft skill side — hope the message lands and the thread of this story comes through. happy reading!

So I just got back from one of my favorite events of the year. It’s different from the usual tech events I attend — this one is centered around women’s empowerment, specifically in Bali. What I love most about it is the call for speakers — giving Balinese women a chance to share their stories on stage. That’s rare outside of the tech space, and it always brings out the most genuinely interesting talks.

Besides the selected speakers, there’s also a special guest invited directly by the committee. This year, it was a friend of mine — not someone my age, already married, and a founder of a Bali-based footwear brand. She talked about life as a business owner and a Balinese wife and mother — where domestic responsibilities aren’t optional. Her session was great, but it ended before I could ask my question.

Fast forward to the break — I ran into her and finally got to ask.

“Hey, I saw on your Instagram that you went to Jakarta for some kind of brand owner event. How did that go? And who invited you in the first place?”

She told me a fellow owner friend brought her along. And once she got there, she picked up insights about branding that she simply wouldn’t have found staying in Bali. Things like how to build and maintain a brand persona that resonates with a wider audience. One thing that really hit her was this realization: a brand is a reflection of its owner. Which meant she had to start showing up — on social media, publicly — even though she’d always been someone who preferred to work behind the scenes.

She came back from Jakarta with more than just a trip. She came back with a new perspective she could actually put into practice.

That conversation stuck with me. It mirrored something I’d decided for myself not too long ago — step outside of Bali and try speaking at events in other cities — not to get famous, not just to travel, but because I knew that staying in the same ecosystem meant I’d keep meeting people learning the same things, at the same level, asking the same questions. And I’d plateau — quietly, without even realizing it.

One of the most memorable experiences was OpenInfra 2025 in Yogyakarta. My first time going to Jogja alone. My first time getting accepted as a speaker at an IT event outside Bali. The community energy there was something else — different from anything I’d felt in my local circle. There’s something a friend once said to me that I still carry:

we don’t share just to get travel support — we share to invest in long-term learning. Because that’s what the process is. We’re exchanging the threads of experience we’ve built through our work.

And honestly, that’s exactly it.

Every time I stand in front of a new audience, I’m not just sharing — I’m learning. From the questions people ask. From the conversations that open up after the session that I never saw coming.

That said — not everyone has the chance to physically step outside their ecosystem right now, and that’s okay. Because learning doesn’t always come in the shape of a plane ticket or a conference stage.

I didn’t start there either. My first step was being invited by a friend to fill a session at a campus event. Nothing fancy. But something grew from that — a sense that showing up isn’t about how expert you are, it’s about being willing to enter a new room.

From there, I started getting more active in online communities. GDG, for example — they have their own channels where you can mingle, listen in on discussions, and meet people who work in the same space but think about it differently. That counts too. That’s already a way of stepping outside your ecosystem.

So if you’re not quite there yet, start with what’s within reach:

  • Listen to stories from people whose path looks different from yours
  • Join an online community that’s slightly outside your comfort zone
  • Say yes to a friend’s invitation — even if you’re not sure it’s relevant

The bigger things tend to show up after you’ve already started moving on the smaller ones.

Your ecosystem isn’t your enemy. But if you only ever live inside it, you’ll never know what you don’t know. The best knowledge and experiences don’t always wait for you somewhere comfortable. Sometimes they’re in a room you’ve never walked into, a city you’ve never visited, or a quick conversation during a coffee break — like the one I had today. So when the chance comes to step outside your ecosystem — take it.

Thanks for reading this far. I don’t always write about soft skills, but when something sticks with me enough to turn into words — I figure it’s worth sharing. Hope it lands for you the way it did for me.

entry.title: How I Nailed My First Three IT Workshops

link.title: How I Nailed My First Three IT Workshops

entry.content:
Hiiii! For now, I’m stepping away from technical content to share something more personal — lessons I learned about soft skills and public speaking. So let’s get right into it.

If you’ve been following my social media — LinkedIn or Instagram — you’ve probably noticed I’ve been invited to speak at three training sessions or workshops. I can hear some of you thinking,

“Just three? That’s not much to brag about.”

You’re right, I’m definitely not a veteran speaker. But since I wanted to contribute and had the bandwidth, I thought, why not? I accepted all opportunities, and I’m happy to report they went really well.

That said, the journey wasn’t all smooth sailing. In the days leading up to each event, my confidence took some serious hits. I even considered backing out at one point, but ultimately stuck with it out of respect for the organizers. Those challenging moments turned out to be incredibly valuable — they taught me lessons that not only got me through those first three workshops but will help me succeed in future speaking engagements.

1. Do Your Homework on the Event

When you get a workshop invitation — whether it’s for a talk, training session, or knowledge-sharing event — dig deep into the details. Who’s organizing it? Is it a university student organization? A professional community? A tech meetup? Understanding the context helps you tailor your content appropriately and figure out what support the organizing team can provide for materials and logistics.

2. Be Smart About Scheduling

As someone working in software development agency, my schedule fluctuates wildly. Some weeks I’m drowning in deliverables, other times it’s relatively calm as we approach project handoffs. Whatever your work situation, be realistic about your availability. If the timing doesn’t work, it’s perfectly acceptable to decline — just do it graciously.

Better yet, when you first receive an invitation, resist the urge to immediately commit or decline. Take 1–2 days to honestly assess your calendar. This prevents you from ghosting organizers later or overcommitting yourself.

3. Keep Your Expectations in Check (Especially as a Beginner)

This one’s crucial. Don’t obsess over attendance numbers. Don’t pester the organizers asking, “How many people have signed up?” Trust me on this — checking registration counts will only psych you out and negatively impact your preparation.

When I was struggling with pre-event jitters before my first workshop, my manager shared a video clip from one of his conference talks. His key message stuck with me:

“So basically, there is no weight parameters that you can use how successful your event. But there is someone else that ask addresses your event is success”
— Mas Doni Rubiagatra at PyCon Korea 2018

Even before that advice, I’d written myself a reminder on X (formerly Twitter) that became my mantra:

“prinsip 1: mau sedikit orang yang dateng, ya tuntun orang itu aja. gak usah punya ekspektasi tinggi bakal banyak yang dateng. apalagi ini pertama kali kamu jadi pemateri di sesi workshop. its okay, kamu bisa sin! kamu punya pengalaman yang related, harusnya kamu bisa!!!”

4. Stay in Your Lane (But Make It Valuable)

Don’t try to teach topics you’re not confident about. Cramming unfamiliar material while juggling a full-time job is a recipe for stress and subpar delivery. Instead, lean into your actual professional experience and knowledge.

For example, if you’re a DevOps engineer, you might cover foundational concepts for beginners or dive into advanced techniques for experienced practitioners — whatever matches both your expertise and your audience’s needs.

5. Go Beyond Slides — Prepare the Full Workshop Experience

Think bigger than just your presentation deck. Do you need external equipment like a projector, adapters, or a laser pointer? Communicate those needs to organizers early. Also prepare supplementary resources: sample code repositories, reference links for post-workshop learning, cheat sheets, etc.

If you have mentors — friends, former professors, significant others, or team leads — who’ve spoken at similar events, pick their brains. Their insights can be invaluable.

6. Train Your Body, Mind, and Voice

Why physical preparation? Because workshops are demanding. You’re not just lecturing — you’re facilitating hands-on exercises, troubleshooting participant issues, and staying on your feet. That’s genuinely tiring.

Mental preparation ensures you can deliver your carefully prepared content clearly and coherently. New to public speaking? Start small: practice presentations with friends, record yourself on camera, or even rehearse in front of a mirror. Seriously, try it — it helps.

7. Spot Your Power Users — And Put Them to Work

Sometimes you’ll encounter participants who are somewhat familiar with your topic, even if they haven’t fully mastered it. Don’t spiral into self-doubt thinking,

“I’m such a fraud. My own attendees know more than me.”

Stop right there — that’s the wrong takeaway.

Instead, view this as a golden opportunity. These participants can be your workshop assistants indirectly. When other attendees struggle, these more experienced folks can step in and help. Think about it from their perspective: they’re reinforcing their existing knowledge by teaching others, which is one of the best ways to solidify learning.

And here’s the bonus: it lightens your workload and helps you manage workshop time more effectively. Everyone wins — participants get peer-to-peer support, your helpers deepen their understanding, and you can focus on keeping the session on track. Pretty smart, right?

Wrapping Up

That got pretty detailed, didn’t it? Well, these are real lessons from real experience. These are the insights I gained while preparing for my first workshop, and they’ve served me well since.

Bottom line: when opportunities come your way, grab them. Speaking engagements build your soft skills portfolio and strengthen your community contributions. Thanks for reading, and catch you in the next post!

entry.title: Dokploy vs Coolify: Real-World Comparison on a Fresh EC2 Instance

link.title: Dokploy vs Coolify: Real-World Comparison on a Fresh EC2 Instance

entry.content:
Back again. Finally writing after my last post about some practical lifehacks. This time, I want to discuss a stack battle — the results of my small research on two popular self-hosted platform alternatives: Dokploy and Coolify.

Why Self-Hosted?

At my workplace, we often get projects that require a combination of SPA/SSR web and a CMS — usually Strapi for the CMS and frameworks like React or Next.js for the web. However, plans are to migrate to PayloadCMS in the future to unify the service across SPA/SSR web and CMS.

So far, the setup process has been done from scratch: install Docker, set up Compose files, sometimes create Swarm clusters for development, staging, and production, then configure the network, Traefik, SSL, and database containers.

While this manual approach gives complete flexibility, I’ve gradually started to feel that there’s one thing that keeps repeating — the same basic setup in every project. From there, I became curious:

“Is there a self-hosted solution that can help speed up the deployment process without sacrificing full control over the environment?”

That’s why I tried two popular tools in this category — Dokploy and Coolify. Both offer a PaaS-like experience similar to Railway or Render, but can be self-hosted on our own servers (e.g., EC2 or VPS).

In this article, I’ll compare my real-world experience installing Dokploy and Coolify on a fresh EC2 instance, and determine whether these platforms are worth it for SPA/SSR + CMS use cases.

Test Setup

For this test, I used:

AWS EC2 t3.Medium

  • 2 vCPU
  • 4 GB RAM
  • Ubuntu 24.04
  • Initial storage: 8 GB (before finally upgrading 😅)
  • Additional: docker and docker compose

Important Note: Minimum Storage

There’s one important thing I discovered during initial testing:

Make sure your VM has at least 16 GB storage.

When I first tried with an 8 GB root volume, the installation process stalled midway, especially during the App service setup phase.

Both platforms, Dokploy and Coolify, don’t just run the leading service but also include supporting components such as internal databases, a Traefik proxy, and backend services. All of this needs extra space.

After I increased the storage to 20GB, the installation process ran smoothly to completion.

Personal tip: If you plan to deploy more than one application (e.g., CMS + frontend + database), it’s safer to allocate 20 GB or more to avoid “No space left on device” errors during the image build process.

Note:

  • If the installation process stops suddenly or a “disk space low” warning appears, it’s most likely that the storage is less than 16 GB.
  • Make sure the root volume is sufficient, because Dokploy and Coolify will automatically run several internal containers.

Installing Dokploy

Both — Dokploy and Coolify — provide an official curl-based one-liner installer.

Let’s start with Dokploy first:

sudo su
curl -fsSL https://dokploy.com/install.sh | bash

The process is relatively fast, about 2–3 minutes on EC2 t3.medium (2 vCPU, 4GB RAM). The developers use Next.js for their dashboard.

The script will automatically:

  • Check if Docker is already installed
  • Pull Dokploy images and their components (Traefik, internal database, backend, frontend dashboard)
  • Run all containers via Docker Compose

After completion, a message like this appears in the terminal:

✅ Dokploy installation finished!
Open http://<your-ec2-ip>:3000 to access the dashboard.

The problem:

By default, port 3000 hasn’t been opened in the EC2 security group, so you can’t directly access the dashboard.

You can work around this by:

  • Manually opening port 3000, or
  • Adding a domain in the Traefik configuration

First impression: Lightweight and fast, but the initial setup is less beginner-friendly.

Bonus: Setting Up Dokploy Domain (Safe & Practical Way)

If you want Dokploy to be immediately accessible via a domain (without IP and port 3000), you can directly modify the Traefik configuration with a single tee command:

sudo tee /etc/dokploy/traefik/dynamic/dokploy.yml > /dev/null << 'EOF'
http:
  routers:
    dokploy-router-app:
      rule: Host(`dokploy.yourdomain.com`)
      service: dokploy-service-app
      entryPoints:
        - web
      middlewares:
        - redirect-to-https
    
    dokploy-router-app-secure:
      rule: Host(`dokploy.yourdomain.com`)
      service: dokploy-service-app
      entryPoints:
        - websecure
      tls:
        certResolver: letsencrypt

  services:
    dokploy-service-app:
      loadBalancer:
        servers:
          - url: http://dokploy:3000
        passHostHeader: true
EOF

Then restart Traefik so the new configuration is loaded:

sudo docker restart dokploy-traefik
sudo docker logs dokploy-traefik --tail 50

If everything goes smoothly, Dokploy can now be accessed and will redirect to the registration page for the first time. Register as usual, and after successful registration, you’ll be directed to the main dashboard:

https://dokploy.yourdomain.com/register
Personal tip: This is the safest and fastest method. After DNS is pointed to your EC2 IP, Dokploy immediately runs via HTTPS with automatic Let’s Encrypt certificate — no additional setup required. However, I hope there will be contributors who can add a “set domain at install time” option to make the initial setup more seamless.

Installing Coolify

The installation steps are almost identical:

curl -fsSL https://cdn.coollabs.io/coolify/install.sh | bash

The process is the same as installing Dokploy (2–3 minutes) because Coolify brings internal components (backend, proxy, DB, UI) along with other development tools like curl, wget, git, jq, and openssl. The developers use PHP for their dashboard.

After completion, the message appears:

Coolify is ready!
Open http://<your-ec2-ip>:8000 to start setup

The problem is the same — port 8000 hasn’t been opened, so the dashboard can’t be accessed yet.

You can:

  • Open port 8000 in the Security Group, or
  • Add a domain via UI, but with SSH Tunnel enabled.

Setting Domain in Coolify (Less Flexible)

Unlike Dokploy, which allows easy direct adjustment of Traefik config, Coolify is not recommended for manual config editing.

Why is Coolify More “Locked Down”?

Technical reasons:

  • Database-driven configuration — All settings are stored in PostgreSQL, not files
  • Auto-generation — Coolify regenerates Traefik config every time there’s a change
  • File overwriting — Manual edits will be overwritten on restart/update
  • State management — Coolify expects it to manage all states

This is a deliberate design choice:

  • Pro: Consistency is maintained, backup/restore is easy, and multi-tenancy is more secure
  • Con: Less flexibility, more complex for quick fixes, steeper learning curve

How to Set Up a Domain in Coolify

Since manual editing is not recommended, we have to use the UI. The problem: port 8000 hasn’t been opened.

Solution: SSH Tunnel

# in your local terminal
ssh -i your-key.pem -L 8000:localhost:8000 ubuntu@<EC2-IP>

Open browser: http://localhost:8000

Steps:

  1. Log in/Register to the Coolify dashboard
  2. Sidebar → Settings → Configuration
  3. In the “Instance’s Domain” field, enter:
https://coolify.yourdomain.com

(Make sure DNS is already pointing to EC2 IP)

4. Click Save

5. Wait ~30–60 seconds

What happens:

  • Coolify updates the database
  • Triggers background job to regenerate Traefik config
  • Requests an SSL certificate via Let’s Encrypt
  • Restarts Traefik proxy
  • Updates routing

Result:

  • Domain live: https://coolify.yourdomain.com
  • No SSH tunnel needed anymore.

Deployment Test: PayloadCMS

After both platforms are successfully accessible via the domain, it’s time to test deployment with a real application: PayloadCMS — one of the popular modern headless CMS for SPA/SSR use cases. I happen to have a custom repo example here.

I’ll test 2 deployment scenarios:

  1. Build from source (GitHub repo → build → deploy)
  2. Pull from registry (Docker image → deploy)

Scenario 1: Build from GitHub Repo

Dokploy Experience

Set up Git Provider

  1. Settings → Git
  2. Select Provider → GitHub (or others as needed)
  3. Klik Create GitHub App
  4. Authorize Dokploy on GitHub
  5. GitHub App connected

Set up Project & Database

  1. Create New Project
  2. Nama project (i.e): payload-cms
  3. Enter project → Create Service → Database → PostgreSQL
  4. Fill in credentials:
Database Name: payload
Username: payload
Password: <generate-strong-password>

5. Click Create → wait for database to be ready (~30 seconds)

Deploy Application

  1. In project → Create Service → Application
  2. App name: payloadcms-app

3. Select Provider → GitHub

4. Select repo: payloadcms (or your template)

5. Branch: main

6. Environment Variables:

DATABASE_URI=postgresql://payload:<password>@postgres:5432/payloaddb
PAYLOAD_SECRET=<random-string-min-32-chars>
NODE_ENV=production

7. Build Settings:

   Build Type: Dockerfile
   Dockerfile Path: ./Dockerfile (or path according to the repository)
   Port: 3000

8. Click Deploy

9. Go to Domains → then change the domain as needed

Build Process:

The application is now live and accessible. On first access, you’ll be redirected to the registration page before you can access the Payload dashboard.

https://payload.yourdomain.com

Resource monitoring:

# Check Dokploy resource usage
docker stats --no-stream | grep dokploy

Result:

root@ip-172-31-36-100:/home/ubuntu# docker stats --no-stream | grep dokploy
CONTAINER ID   NAME                                              CPU %     MEM USAGE / LIMIT     MEM %     NET I/O           BLOCK I/O        PIDS
7be7c038e9b9   dokploy.1.lks1r3j4jh4gftwrluk4um55g                 0.06%     443.4MiB / 3.759GiB   11.52%    21.4MB / 66MB     284MB / 1.97MB   35
900ae1360e84   dokploy-redis.1.ofslueu4i2tmtbnecx38bbv1c           0.51%     6.934MiB / 3.759GiB   0.18%     60.8MB / 16.5MB   16.2MB / 422kB   6
a20680fd1eb8   dokploy-postgres.1.sia2b3a7gasz22eqrl7sl559b        0.00%     29.34MiB / 3.759GiB   0.76%     3.13MB / 3.4MB    37.8MB / 872kB   6
4706ece5e6d8   dokploy-traefik                                     0.00%     53.69MiB / 3.759GiB   1.39%     4.85MB / 6.2MB    138MB / 0B       9

Coolify Experience

Setup Git Provider (GitHub)

  1. Sources → + Add (or New Source)
  2. Select GitHub App
  3. Click Create New GitHub App
  4. Fill GitHub App Name: coolify-<random> (auto-generated)
  5. Click Continue to GitHub → Redirect ke GitHub
  6. Install & authorize on GitHub:
    - Select repositories (All or Select)
    - Click Install
  7. Redirect back to Coolify
  8. GitHub App connected → appears in the Source list

Set up Project & Database

Project Setup:

  1. Projects → + Add (or click New Project)
  2. Fill in project details:
Name: payload-cms
Description: PayloadCMS Deployment (optional)

3. Click Save or Continue

4. Project created → Enter project dashboard

Note: Project is a container for organizing resources (apps, databases, services)

Database Setup:

  1. Inside project → + New → Database
  2. Pilih PostgreSQL
  3. Fill in details:
Name: postgres-db
Database Name: payload
Username: payload
Password: <auto-generated orcustom>
Version: 15 (or latest)

4. (Optional) Set Destination (which server)

5. Klik Save → Start → Database provisioning (~1 minute)

6. Database ready → note the Internal Connection String

Connection String format:

postgresql://payload:<password>@payloaddb:5432/payload

Deploy Application

  1. + New → Resource → Application
  2. Source:
    -     Select the GitHub source created earlier
    - Search & select repo: payloadcms
    - Branch: main
    - Base Directory: /
  3. Build Pack:
    -     Auto-detect: Dockerfile
    - (Or select manual: Nixpacks, Static, Docker Compose)
  4. Tap Continue
  5. Configuration:
    - Port Exposes:     3000
    - Port Mappings:     Leave default or custom

6. Environment Variables:

Tab Environment → Add variables:

DATABASE_URI=postgresql://payload:<password>@payloaddb:5432/payload
PAYLOAD_SECRET=<generate-32-char-random-string>
NODE_ENV=production

Tip: Can use ${SERVICE_PASSWORD_PAYLOADDB} to auto-inject password from database

7. Domains:

  • Add domain: payload.yourdomain.com
  • SSL: Auto (Let’s Encrypt)

8. Click Deploy

Build Process:

Resource monitoring:

root@ip-172-31-34-110:/home/ubuntu# docker stats --no-stream | grep coolify
CONTAINER ID   NAME                                    CPU %     MEM USAGE / LIMIT     MEM %     NET I/O           BLOCK I/O        PIDS
2cf073d978c3   coolify-sentinel                        0.00%     12.5MiB / 3.759GiB    0.32%     34.1kB / 538kB    39.2MB / 0B       8
2846e93a8b06   coolify                                 0.68%     326.1MiB / 3.759GiB   8.47%     2.77GB / 4.47GB   144MB / 120MB     28
a332b2e66451   coolify-realtime                        1.07%     66.5MiB / 3.759GiB    1.73%     1.39MB / 250MB    46MB / 4.1kB      21
e7cf7a4c842e   coolify-redis                           5.48%     9.512MiB / 3.759GiB   0.25%     3.99GB / 1.16GB   14.3MB / 36.2GB   7

e2e211e2c604   coolify-proxy                           0.14%     54.68MiB / 3.759GiB   1.42%     610MB / 281MB     179MB / 41kB      9

Skenario 2: Pull from Docker Registry

Dokploy Experience

As in scenario 1, prior to starting the app setup, you need to prepare the project and database—this process remains unchanged. Once completed, you can proceed to the app setup.

Deploy Application

  1. In project → Create Service → Application
  2. Input Docker Image (i.e): sintiasnn/payload-cms:0.2
  3. Set environment variables
  4. Click Save
  5. Click Deploy

Pull Process:

Important! Dokploy uses a single shared overlay network for all services. This makes inter-service communication simpler, but it comes at the cost of network isolation.

Note: If the image you’re using is private or uses another registry, don’t forget to fill in username, password, and Registry URL for authentication.

Coolify Experience

Similar to scenario 1, before starting the app setup, we need to prepare the project and database. The process is the same as previously. Afterward, we can proceed to the app setup.

Deploy Application

  1. + New → Resource → Application
  2. Source:
    -     Select Docker Image
    - In Image Name, input image name (e.g.): sintiasnn/payload-cms
  3. Tap Continue
  4. Configuration:
    - Port Exposes:     3000
    - Port Mappings:     Leave default or custom

Environment Variables:

Tab Environment → Add variables:

DATABASE_URI=postgresql://payload:<password>@payloaddb:5432/payload
PAYLOAD_SECRET=<generate-32-char-random-string>
NODE_ENV=production

6. Domains:

  • Add domain: payload.yourdomain.com
  • SSL: Auto (Let’s Encrypt)

7. Click Deploy

Pull Process:

Update Experience

Dokploy

Update proses:

  • Push the new commit to GitHub
  • Webhook triggers auto-deploy
  • Zero-downtime deployment via container swap
  • Health check passed → traffic switched

Coolify

Update proses:

  • Git push → auto-deploy
  • Build new image
  • Stop old container → start new
  • Auto DNS update

UI/UX Comparison

Dokploy Dashboard

First impression:

  • Clean, modern (Next.js + Tailwind)
  • Dark mode default
  • Navigation straightforward
  • Mobile responsive

Coolify Dashboard

First impression:

  • Feature-rich
  • Slightly overwhelming at first
  • Many tabs and options
  • Professional look

Final Thoughts: Worth It or Overkill?

Self-hosted deployment platforms like Dokploy and Coolify are indeed game changers. But let’s be honest about one thing:

The resource overhead is not small.

Reality Check

  • Bare minimum spec for both: t3.medium (2 vCPU, 4GB RAM)
  • That’s just for the dashboard. Not yet including the apps you deploy.
  • Worth it? Depends on the use case.

When It’s Worth It?

  • Deploy multiple apps (3–5 apps on one server is cheaper)
  • Deploy frequently (saves 2+ hours of setup per project)
  • Need reproducible setup (moving servers requires restoring config)

Sweet spot: 2–5 small-scale applications like PayloadCMS, Next.js sites, APIs.

When It’s Overkill

  • Only one small app (manual deployment is cheaper)
  • Budget < $20/month (resource overhead is too expensive)
  • Rarely deploy (manual setup effort is still worth it)

Important Note: Scaling

  • Dokploy uses Docker Swarm — theoretically can be multi-node, but the UI doesn’t yet fully support node management. Hopefully, future updates will expose more Swarm features.
  • Coolify focuses on a single server. Want to scale? Set up multiple instances, not a cluster.

Reality: For “saving resources,” neither is ideal yet. The dashboard alone needs 2–4GB of RAM.

Personal Take

For small-scale applications like PayloadCMS? Worth it if you have 2+ apps. But don’t expect “resource savings” — this is about saving setup time. Neither is bad. It comes back to your needs.

Happy experimenting! Have you tried Dokploy or Coolify yet? Drop your experience in the comments — I’d love to know which one worked better for your use case. Thanks for reading!

Resources

  • Dokploy GitHub
  • Coolify GitHub
  • PayloadCMS

<hr><p>Dokploy vs Coolify: Real-World Comparison on a Fresh EC2 Instance was originally published in Zero One Group on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.</p>

entry.title: My Favourite AWS CLI Lifehack: Profile Switching with Oh My Zsh

link.title: My Favourite AWS CLI Lifehack: Profile Switching with Oh My Zsh

entry.content:
If you work with AWS daily (devops, cloud engineer, etc), especially if you manage more than one account, you’re likely familiar with the hassle of switching profiles in the AWS CLI. I’ve been there myself. I once had a critical moment on a project where I almost provisioned infrastructure to the wrong environment. The cause was simple: I forgot to switch the active AWS credential.

That incident got me thinking, “There has to be a more efficient way to switch profiles.” After conducting some research, I finally found the solution, which turned out to be in a tool I already use every day: Oh My Zsh.

This feature completely changed my workflow, making the process of switching accounts incredibly fast and safe. Today, I want to share this practical guide with you.

What You’ll Need

Before we dive into the configuration, make sure you have these two tools installed on your computer:

  1. Oh My Zsh: A framework for Zsh (Z shell) that makes your terminal more powerful and easier to customise. If you’re still using the standard bash shell, I highly recommend giving it a try.
  2. AWS CLI: The official command-line interface from AWS for interacting with its various services. You can follow the official installation guide here.

All set? Let’s get started!

Step 1: Enable the aws Plugin in Your Zsh Configuration

To make the magic happen, we need to tell Oh My Zsh to enable its AWS plugin. Often, this plugin is not enabled by default.

It’s very easy to set up:

  1. Open the .zshrc file located in your home directory. You can use any text editor you like (nano, vim, or VS Code).
  2. Find the line that contains plugins=(...).
  3. Add aws to the list of plugins. If you already have other plugins (like git), add it alongside them.
# Example .zshrc content
plugins=(git aws)

4. Save the file, then reload your terminal configuration by running:

source ~/.zshrc

Step 2: Set Up Your Profiles in the AWS Config Directory

Now for the most important part. The AWS CLI stores all your account configurations in a folder named ~/.aws. Inside, there are two key files we need to set up: credentials and config.

1. The credentials File

Think of this file as a secure wallet for your secret access keys. It stores the aws_access_key_id and aws_secret_access_key for each account.

IMPORTANT: Because this file contains sensitive data, never share its contents with anyone!

Open the ~/.aws/credentials file and set it up like the example below. Each account is separated by a [profile-name].

[default]
aws_access_key_id = AKIAIOSFODNN7EXAMPLE
aws_secret_access_key = wJalrXUtnFEMI/K7MDENG/bPxRfiCYEXAMPLEKEY

[project-a]
aws_access_key_id = AKIAI44QH8DHBEXAMPLE
aws_secret_access_key = je7MtGbClwBF/2Zp9Utk/h3yCo8nvbEXAMPLEKEY

[project-b-sandbox]
aws_access_key_id = AKIA3IT55L4A4EXAMPLE
aws_secret_access_key = 5i/raJx4ottp8kZTu16j6TGN2iLoEXAMPLEKEY

2. The config File

This file is used to store non-sensitive settings, such as the default region or output format for each profile. The format is similar to the credentials file, but the profile name is prefixed with the word profile.

Open the ~/.aws/config file and align it with the profiles you created earlier.

[default]
region = ap-southeast-1
output = json

[profile project-a]
region = us-east-1
output = json

[profile project-b-sandbox]
region = ap-southeast-3
output = text
  • region: Sets the default AWS region when you run commands for that profile.
  • output: Configures the output format from CLI commands (commonly json, text, or table).

How to Use It: Meet the Magic Commands

Once everything is configured, the Oh My Zsh aws plugin provides several helpful aliases (command shortcuts). These commands work by setting the AWS_PROFILE environment variable for your terminal session.

asp (AWS Set Profile)

This is your main command for switching profiles.

  • To List Profiles: Type asp followed by a space, then press the Tab key. Oh My Zsh will show you all available profiles.
$ asp <press Tab>
default             project-a
  • To Activate a Profile: Specify the name of the profile you want to use.
$ asp project-a
AWS profile set to 'project-a'

agp (AWS Get Profile)

This command is useful for checking which profile is currently active.

  • Usage:
$ agp
project-

unset-aws-profile

If you want to return to the default profile or simply deactivate the current one, use this command.

  • Usage:
$ unset-aws-profile
AWS profile unset

With these three simple commands, switching between AWS accounts becomes incredibly fast and safe. Say goodbye to the risk of deploying to the wrong environment!

Happy coding, and I hope this tip makes your workflow more efficient!

entry.title: Your journey to the cloud: Starting with Linux and Building Simple APIs

link.title: Your journey to the cloud: Starting with Linux and Building Simple APIs

entry.content:
This story began when I had the opportunity to be a mentor at a workshop. They asked me to present a session on cloud computing. However, I felt it wouldn’t make sense to jump straight into cloud providers. Here’s why — when people hear the word ‘cloud,’ the first thing that comes to their mind is…

“How do you use GCP? How do you use AWS?”

But if you want to dive into cloud computing, you should first get familiar with computers and their operating systems. And what else could it be if not Linux? That operating system where everything is done through the command prompt😜

As an Infrastructure Engineer who started my career directly in a cloud provider, I realized that Linux fundamentals are essential and serve as the very foundation of cloud computing. To ensure people don’t take the wrong path, I decided to cover this topic. Since only the workshop participants had access to the material at the time, I chose to adapt my presentation into an article. You can check out a snippet of the workshop in this post! 😁

Post | Feed | LinkedIn

It might feel repetitive, especially when covering basic Linux concepts, but that’s okay. As long as the readers can understand it, I’m happy to present this topic again. In this article, I’ll guide you through the basics of Linux and show you how to run a simple API directly in Linux using PM2.

This article will be divided into several sections, including:

  • What is Linux? Why is it so Important in your Cloud Journey?
  • Explorating Linux CLI based in hand-on-labs
  • Building and running simple APIs in Linux

Are you curious? Alright, let’s dive into the first section

What is Linux? Why is it so Important in your Cloud Journey?

Linux is an open-source OS kernel that serves as the foundation for a wide range of operating systems. It was developed by Linus Torvalds in 1991. Since then it has evolved into one of the most powerful OS available used in various scenarios, including servers, cloud computing, DevOps, and IoT. [1]

Linux is Important in your Cloud Journey because...

  • Widespread Adoption in Cloud Infrastructure: Many cloud services like AWS, GCP, and Azure use Linux as their primary operating system.
  • Supports DevOps and Automation: Linux provides tools like Bash, Ansible, and Docker that simplify automation and infrastructure management.
  • Compatibility with Cloud-Native Technologies: Kubernetes, Docker, and microservices-based services are built on Linux.
  • Flexibility and Security: Linux has a strong permission management system and can be customized as needed.

Due to the important role of Linux, I want to emphasize to you — the readers of this article — the importance of mastering Linux fundamentals, so you don’t end up like the meme below.

Especially for those pursuing a career in infrastructure, this article may not cover everything. But don’t worry — you can continue learning through roadmap.sh (Linux Roadmap).

Besides the basic commands we’ll cover in the next section, there are several other important topics worth exploring. More importantly, on roadmap, you’ll find reference links (such as blogs or courses) that can further enhance your knowledge.

Alright! We’ve completed the first section — let’s move on to the second one.

Explorating Linux CLI based in hand-on-labs

Before getting started, ensure you have access to a Linux environment, either through WSL (Windows Subsystem for Linux) or SSH into a remote server.

Linux Directory Structure

The first thing that Linux beginners need to understand is the folder structure, commonly referred to as Directories. Just like in other operating systems, each directory has its specific role. Here are some key directories in Linux:

Basic Linux Commands

If you have already grasped the principles of directories in Linux, the next step is to familiarize yourself with the basic commands that every Linux user should know. These commands are crucial for understanding how this operating system works as a whole. Furthermore, the command line allows users to access functions that are often unavailable in the graphical interface. Here are some essential commands you can try.

Shell scripting

A shell script is a computer program designed to be run by a Unix shell. It’s a sequence of commands that the shell interprets and executes. Shell scripts are often used for automation, system administration, and other tasks. Shell scripting usually has the extension .sh behind the file name. Here’s an example of a file that implements shell scripting.

The first line of a script contains the syntax #!/bin/bash, which is used to call the Bash shell. Alternatively, you can use #!/bin/sh it if you want to create a generic script that is compatible across various operating systems. This is followed by additional commands, allowing you to combine the basic commands you have learned into a shell script to streamline the execution of multiple commands at once.

It’s important to note that the file is typically not executable when you first create a shell script. To make the script executable, you must modify the file’s permissions using the chmod command. For example:

chmod +x script.sh

Package management

On Linux, software is typically built as a package, distributed through repositories, and managed on the end-user’s system through package managers. Package management in Linux is the process of managing software in the system, including the installation, update, configuration, and removal of packages. Each Linux distribution usually has its own package management system with different formats and tools.

  • APT (for Debian and Ubuntu)
  • DNF (for RHEL/CentOS 8 and Fedora 22 or latest)
  • YUM (for earlier versions of RHEL/CentOS and Fedora)

Because we use the Ubuntu Distro in our workshop, we will use APT for package management. The following commands are often used in APT.

Build and run simple APIs in Linux

We’ve reached the practical session, which is also the final segment of this workshop. In this session, we will build and run an API using PM2 directly on Linux. This guide will walk us through setting up and running a simple API using Node.js, pnpm, and PM2 in a Linux environment. Let’s get started!

Step 1: Setup Prerequisites

Install Node.js

Official Guide

sudo apt-get install -y curl
curl -fsSL https://deb.nodesource.com/setup_23.x -o nodesource_setup.sh
sudo -E bash nodesource_setup.sh
sudo apt-get install -y nodejs
node -v

Install pnpm

Official Guide

curl -fsSL https://get.pnpm.io/install.sh | sh -

Install Git

sudo apt update
sudo apt install git -y

Step 2: Setup the Project

Clone the Repository

# Using SSH
git clone git@github.com:sintiasnn/example-api.git <your-directory>

# Using HTTPS
git clone https://github.com/sintiasnn/example-api.git <your-directory>
Note: Ensure your SSH key is registered with GitHub. You can generate an SSH key using:
ssh-keygen -t rsa -b 4096 -C "your_email@example.com"
Then, add the generated id_rsa.pub key to your GitHub account. Follow the guide here.

Install Dependencies and initiate PM2

cd <your-directory>
pnpm install
pnpm install pm2 -g
pm2 init

Edit ecosystem.config.cjs for PM2 Configuration

vi ecosystem.config.cjs
module.exports = {
  apps: [{
    name: "my-backend",
    script: "./server.js",
    env: {
      NODE_ENV: "production",
      PORT: 3002,
      HOSTNAME: "127.0.0.1"
    }
  }]
};

Step 3: Run Your API with PM2

Start the API

pm2 start ecosystem.config.cjs

Check the Status in out PM2

pm2 status

Test the API using curl

curl 127.0.0.1:3002

Stop the API

pm2 stop ecosystem.config.cjs

Step 4: Adjust Your API

Edit server.js

vi server.js
// Import the framework and instantiate it
import Fastify from "fastify";
const fastify = Fastify({
  logger: true
});

// Declare a route
fastify.get("/", async function handler(request, reply) {
  # change welcomeSentence
  return { welcomeSentence: "Hello World from Fastify!" };
});

// Run the server!!
try {
  await fastify.listen({ port: process.env.PORT, host: process.env.HOSTNAME });
} catch (err) {
  fastify.log.error(err);
  process.exit(1);
}

Update ecosystem.config.cjs

vi ecosystem.config.cjs
module.exports = {
  apps: [{
        name: "my-backend",   # you can adjust name server
        script: "./server.js",
        env: {
            NODE_ENV: "production",
            PORT: 3003,   #change port to anticipate conflict
            HOSTNAME: "127.0.0.1"
        }
  }]
};

Restart the API

pm2 start ecosystem.config.cjs

Test Using the New Port

curl 127.0.0.1:3003

Stop the API

pm2 stop ecosystem.config.cjs

Conclusion

Congratulations! You have successfully built and deployed a simple application on Linux. Throughout this journey, we’ve learned a lot, from an introduction to Linux, the key reasons why Linux serves as the foundation of cloud computing, practicing basic commands, and a brief overview of package management to hands-on experience in building and running applications with PM2. I hope this article is useful for you, and stay tuned for my next articles. See you soon!

References

How to Manage User Permissions with the GUI in Linux

Basic Linux Commands

Linux File and Directory Operations

Linux Introduction to Linux

Ubuntu Package Management

Linux Package Management Overview

File System Hierarchy Standard (FHS)

Introduction to Linux Shell and Shell Scripting

Shell Scripting Basics

entry.title: Bangkit Story — Week 2
entry.content:
Bangkit Story — Week 2

Hi Everyone. I hope everyone who reads this blog is always healthy. I will continue to write about my experiences during Bangkit Academy. Before that, I apologize to the readers for delaying the creation of this blog because I have something to do from campus. Alright, let’s move on to the main topic.

what have I learned during the second week?

During the second week, I continued to study the Basic Learning Web Programming module on the Dicoding web platform. in this module, I learn more about flexbox and basic javascript. At the end of the module, there is a final exam and submission task to find out how well you understand the material being studied and the requirements for getting a certificate.

The submission task in the basic learning module of web programming is to create a simple web with some conditions such as applying HTML semantics, there are all required elements (for example Header, Footer, Main, Article, and Aside), there is an identity for the aside element, and applying float and flexbox.

In this submission, I created a landing page with the title miana world. The reason I created this landing page is that I am interested in miana plants (a type of mint). In practice, this landing page applies basic HTML and basic CSS.

The full details are in my Github repository. you can see it in the link.

After I submitted the results of the landing page that I made, it turned out that my submission was approved by getting a rating of 5. This is because it has met the initial requirements as well as several additional requirements such as colour combinations and others. So that I can pass on this module. Credentials can be seen on the link.

Also in the second week, I studied the Basic Learning Javascript programming module. In this module, I learned many things about javascript such as javascript fundamentals(variable, data type, operator, if/else, loop), data structures(array, object, spread operator, map, set), functions(declaration function, function parameters , arrow function, variable scope, closure), object-oriented programming(class, property & method, 4 pillars of oop, overriding method, object composition), functional programming(functional programming concepts), setup environment(node.js), modules( export-import class), and error handling(try and catch, throwing errors, and custom errors).

On February 24, 2022, ILT-CC-01 or Instructor Lead-Cloud Computing series 1 was held via google meet. This session was attended by groups CC-37, CC-38 and CC-39 guided by Kak Inggih Wicaksono. The material presented is about the basics of HTML and Javascript. The instructor gives a demo program so that it can be understood by students.

In addition, the first weekly consultation session was carried out by the facilitator with CC-38 friends (my group). This session discusses the progress of students during learning and the technical obstacles encountered by students. Because it’s only the first week, we open this session with self-introductions.

I feel happy because I get new insights and can discuss with friends if problems are found while studying. Hopefully, this blog is useful for readers. I apologize if there are mistakes in terms of phrases, grammar, paraphrasing or others. See you in the next blog.

And don’t forget,
Thank you Bangkit for the opportunity

#SinsinBangkit2022Story
